clue.text: Pet with clothing, belly out, is comical

parts.note: Jo is an old Scots word for a sweetheart or darling, a pet

indicators.note: out tells us the belly word is taken away from the clothing word

parts.note: a costume is a set of clothing
tum is a colloquial word for the belly

explanation.surface: A pet animal in a little outfit, its tummy poking out, is a funny sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes TUM from COSTUME, leaving COSE. JO (from Burns, 'John Anderson, my jo') is an obscure word for a sweetheart.
explanation.definitionFit: Jocose describes someone playful and joking, which is a synonym for funny or comical.

clue.text: DA then re-engineered fan

indicators.note: the letters are engineered into a new structure, the second half of 're-engineered' working as the anagram signal

explanation.surface: A district attorney who has been reprogrammed into a devoted supporter.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated word is split: its 're' joins DA THEN as fodder and 'engineered' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A fan of something is a follower or supporter of it, a synonym of an adherent.

clue.text: Boatman's upper crust, bleeding edge, going forward

definitions.note: read as 'Boatman is': the setter calls himself a sailor, and an ordinary sailor in the navy is called this

indicators.note: the edge letter of the crust word bleeds away from its place in the word
the edge letter goes forward through the word to its far end, a business-jargon phrase reused

parts.note: a gratin is a dish with a browned crust of breadcrumbs or cheese on top

explanation.surface: Business-speak: the setter is cutting-edge elite from now on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bleeding edge' and 'going forward' are business jargon, the puzzle's theme. Together they move the G at the edge of GRATIN to the other end. 'Boatman's' is the definition, the setter naming himself as a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A rating is a non-commissioned sailor, so a boatman, which the setter's pseudonym says he is, is one.

clue.text: In your mouth, it's tender fruitless sweet spot

parts.note: a fruit gum is a chewy sweet; take 'fruit' away and the gum remains
a boil is a painful spot on the skin

explanation.surface: A dentist's warning: there's a sore place in your mouth where sweets have done damage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fruitless sweet' is a fruit gum without the fruit. A fruit gum is a British chewy sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: A gumboil is an abscess on the gum, a sore swelling felt inside the mouth.

clue.text: Perhaps Betty Moon? Heads up for plant needed to get well

indicators.note: in a down clue, sending the pieces up the column reads them backwards

parts.note: Betty is an example of a girl's name, so a girl
Io is one of the moons of Jupiter

explanation.surface: A woman called Betty Moon is warned to look out for a plant that will help her recover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads up' reverses GIRL + IO in this down clue. 'well' is an oil well, not good health.
explanation.definitionFit: An oil rig is industrial equipment, a plant, that drills to reach an oil well.

clue.text: Dead unimportant

definitions.meaning: vital can mean alive, so dead is lacking life

explanation.surface: A slangy pairing, as in 'dead boring', meaning really unimportant.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a surface, 'Dead' is an intensifier ('dead easy'); as a definition it means lifeless, the opposite of 'vital' in its living sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Vital means both living and essential, so its negation fits both lifeless and inessential.

clue.text: Popularly priced and in vogue — load up

indicators.note: up here means amiss or wrong, as in 'what's up?', so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Something cheap and fashionable, so stock up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' as an anagram signal means amiss (the setter defended it on the blog); 'and in' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worth what it costs, at a price people like, is reasonably priced and so popular.

clue.text: One closes loop — how synergy begins, where people take the plunge

parts.note: a lid is a thing that closes a container
the letter O is shaped like a loop

indicators.note: begins asks for the first letter of the word synergy

explanation.surface: Business jargon: someone who closes the loop is where synergy starts and people take bold risks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'closes the loop' and 'synergy' are business jargon, the puzzle's theme. 'take the plunge' means dive into water, not risk something new.
explanation.definitionFit: Lidos are public open-air swimming pools, places where swimmers dive in.

clue.text: Arms for long distance backed by nonsense talk

indicators.note: by places the nonsense after the reversed distance
backed means the distance word is turned round

parts.note: a mile is a long distance
BS is a slang abbreviation for nonsense, short for bullshit

explanation.surface: Weapons for long-range use, supported by meaningless chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arms' looks like weapons but means limbs; 'backed' makes ELIM from MILE.
explanation.definitionFit: Forelimbs are the front legs of an animal, and in a person they are the arms.

clue.text: Push the envelope of danger: Boatman's following

indicators.note: following puts the setter's piece after the outer letters
the envelope is the outer wrapping, so the outside letters of danger

parts.note: the setter's 'Boatman has' becomes 'I've' from the setter's own point of view

explanation.surface: Jargon: the setter is pushing the envelope of danger next.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Push the envelope' is business jargon; here 'envelope' signals the outer letters DR. 'Boatman's' means 'Boatman has', giving I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive cattle or a nail is to push it forward, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Sly to reach out pointlessly

indicators.note: out means out of order, so the letters are rearranged
a compass point, here east, is lost from the word reach

explanation.surface: A crafty person stretches out without purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pointlessly' removes E (east, a compass point) from REACH; 'out' shuffles RACH.
explanation.definitionFit: Arch as an adjective means knowing and mischievous, close to sly or roguish.

clue.text: Witness reported beggar, uncovered disposing of a spiky urchin

indicators.note: reported means the word is heard, spoken aloud

parts.note: to witness something is to see it

indicators.note: disposing of means the letter a is thrown out
uncovered strips off the outside letters of beggar

explanation.surface: A witness says a ragged beggar was stripped of his rags by a street child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncovered' turns BEGGAR into EGGA, then 'disposing of a' leaves EGG. 'urchin' looks like a street child, but it is the sea creature.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea egg is a name for the sea urchin, a spiny marine animal.

clue.text: Out of repair, rig a technical means to supply water

indicators.note: the letters come out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Using parts from a repair job, rigging up a technical means of piping water.
explanation.definitionFit: To irrigate land is to bring water to it through channels or pipes.

clue.text: Paradigm shift in poem: it has terminal consonance

indicators.note: a shift moves things around, so the letters of poem and it are rearranged
terminal asks for the final letter of consonance

explanation.surface: A poem changing its model, its endings rhyming in consonance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paradigm shift' is business jargon split in two: 'Paradigm' is the definition and 'shift' the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A paradigm is a perfect model or example, as an epitome is the typical embodiment of something.

clue.text: Not a ham, as ham might be supplied for immoral acts

parts.note: a ham is an amateur performer, so not one is a professional, a pro
ham meat is often cured by salting or smoking

explanation.surface: A real actor, not an amateur, provided as a meat might be for wicked purposes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ham' means an amateur performer the first time, cured meat the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To procure is to obtain someone for prostitution, providing them for sexual immorality.

clue.text: My agile, lean thoughtful leadership could be moonshine

indicators.note: the leaders of the words are their first letters, a business-jargon word reused

explanation.surface: Jargon: my agile, lean, thoughtful leadership style might be nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'agile', 'lean' and 'leadership' are business jargon; 'moonshine' means illicit liquor here, not foolish talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Malt whisky is distilled liquor, and moonshine is illicitly distilled spirit, so it could be one.

clue.text: Run away from (rudely snub) Harlem Shuffle

indicators.note: rudely means roughly, so the letters are roughly mixed up
the letters of run go away from the mixed letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Fleeing from a rude rebuff, someone dances the Harlem Shuffle.
explanation.walkthrough: SNUB HARLEM, shuffled with 'rudely', holds SHAMBLE plus RUN, which 'away from' removes. Harlem Shuffle is a 1960s soul song; 'Run' is a word, not just R.
explanation.definitionFit: To shamble is to walk awkwardly, dragging the feet, the same gait as a shuffle.

clue.text: For big business leaders, change management's losing men

indicators.note: change means alter the order of the letters
losing means the letters of men are left out of the mix

explanation.surface: Bosses order a restructure that sheds male staff.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the letters of the possessive word, less the men, are mixed by 'change'.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnates are tycoons, wealthy and powerful figures who run major companies.

clue.text: Terrain reimagined for coach

indicators.note: reimagined means thought up anew, so the letters are given a new order

explanation.surface: Landscape redesigned for a bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coach' looks like a bus but is a sports instructor.
explanation.definitionFit: A coach is someone who instructs athletes, a synonym of a sports instructor.

clue.text: One gets beneath the surface of cannabis, uncovering disease

parts.note: pot is a slang word for cannabis

indicators.note: uncovering means the outer letters of the disease are stripped away

parts.note: cholera is an infectious disease

explanation.surface: A drug user digs into the problem, revealing illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncovering' strips C and A off CHOLERA, leaving HOLER. 'One gets beneath the surface' sounds like an investigator.
explanation.definitionFit: A potholer explores caves, literally going underground beneath the ground's surface.

clue.text: Core competency raised — leader embraces it, excited

indicators.note: embraces means the leader word holds the other piece

parts.note: a head is a leader

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means read upwards, backwards
the core is the middle, so the central letters of competency

explanation.surface: Jargon: a boss is thrilled that the team's core competency has gone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Core' gives ET from COMPETENCY; 'raised' turns it to TE in this down clue; 'embraces' puts it into HEAD. 'Core competency' is business jargon.
explanation.definitionFit: Heated means passionate or roused, as an argument is heated when tempers are worked up.

clue.text: Following scrap, you say your leader is fit for heavy lifting?

indicators.note: you say means the word is spoken aloud

parts.note: a mite is a tiny scrap or bit

indicators.note: the leader is the first letter of your

explanation.surface: After a fight, you claim your boss is strong enough to lift weights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scrap' looks like a fight but means a tiny bit, a mite.
explanation.definitionFit: Mighty means very strong, so able to lift heavy loads.

clue.text: Insubordination in Spain's greatly outside the box

indicators.note: outside puts the Spanish word around the box

parts.note: muy is Spanish for very or greatly
a tin is a box

explanation.surface: Rebellion in Spain is a matter of thinking outside the box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside the box' is business jargon, split so that 'outside' is the container signal and 'the box' a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: A mutiny is an open revolt against officers, the most extreme disobedience.

clue.text: Compact lunch, say, consumed by judge

indicators.note: consumed by means the eating word goes inside the judging word

parts.note: to try a case is to judge it
to lunch is an example of eating

explanation.surface: A small packed lunch is eaten by a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compact' looks like an adjective but is a noun, a pact; 'lunch' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: A compact is an agreement between parties, a formal treaty or pact.

clue.text: Buzzword for one thing that bosses and workers all are

definitions.text: thing that bosses and workers all are

parts.note: read as 'buzz word', a word for a buzz: a hum is a low buzzing noise
an is the indefinite article, meaning one of something

explanation.surface: Jargon: the latest buzzword for something every boss and worker shares.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buzzword' looks like the theme's jargon, but is read as a word meaning buzz. 'one thing' is a person, used loosely as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyone in an office, manager or staff, is a person, a member of our species.

clue.text: Added volume in disrupted arterial transport mode

indicators.note: added tells us the volume letter is put into the mixed letters
in places the volume letter within the disrupted letters
disrupted means the letters of arterial are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Extra traffic on a congested main road makes a different way of getting about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arterial' suggests a main road, but its letters are mixed by 'disrupted', and V goes into ARTRAEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Flying is a way of getting from place to place, one way to travel.

clue.text: Cut hard at the end of the day

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

indicators.note: end of asks for the last letter of the word the

parts.note: Wed is the abbreviation for Wednesday, a day

explanation.surface: Jargon: at the end of the day, the cut was a tough one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at the end of the day' is business jargon split up: 'at' links, 'end of the' gives E, 'day' gives WED.
explanation.definitionFit: To hew is to chop with an axe, so the past form means chopped.

clue.text: Check places for funds again

parts.note: to rein in is to check or restrain
to vest power in someone is to place it with them

explanation.surface: An inspector looks at where the money has gone a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'funds' is a verb here, and 'places' a verb meaning puts.
explanation.definitionFit: To put money back into a business is to finance it a second time.
